summary: Describes obsolete syntax that IMAP4 implementations might meet when dealing with older versions of the Internet Mail Access Protocol. It is informational and meant to help with compatibility.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP is the protocol a mail program uses to fetch mail from a server. Over the years a few commands changed or disappeared. This memo collects the old forms so that a server can still talk to an old client if it wants to, and so that a client knows what to ignore.

subtitle: The old IMAP4 commands and responses that a server may still meet, and need not support.

tldr.problem: A new IMAP4 server can still meet clients that speak the older syntax, and needs to know what to do about them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the commands, fetch data items and responses that were made obsolete, together with the rule that new servers must not send the obsolete responses but client implementations should still accept them.
tldr.outcome: A server may implement the obsolete syntax if it wants better interoperability with old clients, but is not required to, and the rules for the obsolete responses are one way: servers must not send them, clients must cope with them.

today: RFC 2062 is an Informational memo from December 1996, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion document to the main IMAP4 specification, listing the syntax that IMAP4 dropped and that a server may still implement for compatibility with old clients.

sections.title: Why the Memo Exists
sections.content:
This document describes obsolete syntax which may be encountered by IMAP4 implementations that deal with older versions of the Internet Message Access Protocol. IMAP4 implementations may implement this syntax in order to maximize interoperability with older implementations. It repeats information from earlier documents, most notably RFC 1176 and RFC 1730.

The memo is a companion to the main IMAP4 document rather than a protocol in its own right. It lists commands, fetch data items and responses that are marked OBSOLETE, and states that it is not required to support any of these commands or fetch data items in new server implementations. They are documented here for the benefit of implementors who may wish to support them for compatibility with old client implementations. The section headings of these commands are intended to correspond with where they would be located in the main document if they were not obsoleted, so the numbering carries gaps and the suffix OBS.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here is required. The memo exists so that an implementor who chooses to support the old forms knows exactly what they are.

sections.title: The Obsolete Commands
sections.content:
Four commands are listed as obsolete. FIND ALL.MAILBOXES takes a mailbox name with possible wildcards and returns untagged MAILBOX replies. It returns a subset of names from the complete set of all names available to the user, and its mailbox argument is similar to that for LIST with an empty reference, except that the characters % and ? match a single character. The result is OK when the find completed, NO when the find failed because that name cannot be listed, and BAD when the command is unknown or its arguments are invalid.

FIND MAILBOXES works the same way but returns a subset of the names the user has declared as being active or subscribed. Its mailbox argument is similar to that for LSUB with an empty reference, with the same % and ? wildcards, and it also returns untagged MAILBOX replies.

SUBSCRIBE MAILBOX and UNSUBSCRIBE MAILBOX are identical in effect to SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE, and both take a mailbox name as their argument. A server that implements them must be able to distinguish between a SUBSCRIBE MAILBOX command and a SUBSCRIBE command with a mailbox name argument of MAILBOX, and the same distinction is needed for UNSUBSCRIBE. That matters because MAILBOX is itself a possible mailbox name.
sections.plainLanguage: The FIND commands list mailboxes by pattern, and the SUBSCRIBE MAILBOX commands are older spellings of SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE. A server that accepts them has to be able to tell them apart from the ordinary commands with a mailbox named MAILBOX.

sections.title: The PARTIAL Command and the Obsolete Fetch Items
sections.content:
The PARTIAL command takes a message sequence number, a message data item name, the position of the first octet and the number of octets, and returns untagged FETCH responses. It is equivalent to the associated FETCH command with the added functionality that only the specified number of octets, beginning at the specified starting octet, are returned. Only a single message can be fetched at a time, and the first octet of a message is octet 1. The valid data for PARTIAL are RFC822, RFC822.HEADER, RFC822.TEXT and BODY[section], as well as any .PEEK forms of these.

Any partial fetch that attempts to read beyond the end of the text is truncated as appropriate, and if the starting octet is beyond the end of the text an empty string is returned. The data come back in the FETCH response, and there is no indication of the range of the partial data in that response. It is not possible to stream multiple PARTIAL commands of the same data item without processing and synchronizing at each step, since streamed commands may be executed out of order. There is no requirement that partial fetches follow any sequence, so if a partial fetch of octets 1 through 10000 breaks in an awkward place for BASE64 decoding, it is permitted to continue with a partial fetch of 9987 through 19987. The handling of the \Seen flag is the same as in the associated FETCH command.

Five fetch data items are also obsolete. BODY[...]0, a body part number of 0, is the RFC-822 header of the message and is functionally equivalent to BODY[HEADER], differing in the syntax of the resulting untagged FETCH data. RFC822.HEADER.LINES is functionally equivalent to BODY.PEEK[HEADER.LINES], and RFC822.HEADER.LINES.NOT to BODY.PEEK[HEADER.LINES.NOT]. RFC822.PEEK is functionally equivalent to BODY.PEEK[], and RFC822.TEXT.PEEK to BODY.PEEK[TEXT]. In every case the difference is the syntax of the untagged FETCH data that comes back.
sections.plainLanguage: PARTIAL fetches a chosen stretch of a message, such as the first thousand bytes, so a client does not have to download the whole thing. The old fetch names do the same job under a different spelling.

sections.title: The Obsolete Responses
sections.content:
Three responses are obsolete. Except as noted below, these responses must not be transmitted by new server implementations, and client implementations should accept them.

The MAILBOX response carries a name. It must not be transmitted by server implementations except in response to the obsolete FIND MAILBOXES and FIND ALL.MAILBOXES commands, and client implementations that do not use those commands may ignore it. It returns a single name that matches the FIND specification, with no attributes and no hierarchy delimiter.

The COPY response carries no data. It must not be transmitted by new server implementations, and client implementations must ignore it. In some experimental versions of the protocol this response was returned in response to a COPY command to indicate, on a per-message basis, that the message was copied successfully.

The STORE response carries message data. It must not be transmitted by new server implementations, and client implementations must treat it as equivalent to the FETCH response. In some experimental versions of the protocol this response was returned instead of FETCH in response to a STORE command, to report the new value of the flags.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule for these three is one-sided. A server must not send them, but a client must still cope if an old server does.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The memo gives the formal syntax rules for the obsolete commands and responses. Each rule suffixed with _old is added to the corresponding name in the formal syntax, so command_auth_old adds the FIND command to command_auth, and command_select_old adds PARTIAL to command_select.

The rules define find as FIND, optionally ALL., then MAILBOXES and a list_mailbox; partial as PARTIAL, a non-zero number, a fetch_text_old and two numbers; subscribe_old and unsubscribe_old as the SUBSCRIBE or UNSUBSCRIBE command followed by MAILBOX and a mailbox; fetch_att_old and fetch_text_old for the old fetch item names; msg_data_old for COPY and for STORE followed by a message attribute; section_old as a bracket containing an optional dotted number; and date_year_old and date_time_old for the date rules.

The zone_name rule lists the time zone names the protocol understands: UT, GMT and Z for plus zero; AST, EDT, EST, CDT, CST, MDT, MST, PDT, PST, YDT, YST, HDT, HST, BDT and BST for the North American offsets from minus four to minus eleven; and the single letters A through Y, skipping J, for offsets of plus one to plus twelve and minus one to minus twelve.
sections.plainLanguage: The last part of the memo is the grammar, so that a parser can be written from it. Each old rule is added to the modern one under a name ending in _old.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Status
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The status statement says that the memo provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and that its distribution is unlimited.

The memo closes with the author's address at the University of Washington, and repeats information from earlier documents, most notably RFC 1176 and RFC 1730.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing about security here. The memo is a reference for implementors, not a standard to be met.
